narrative_stages.label: Origin
narrative_stages.headline: Started in a garage, helped invent the PC industry
narrative_stages.detail: Apple was founded in 1976, and its early Macintosh computers helped invent the idea of a personal computer built for ordinary people, not just engineers and hobbyists.

narrative_stages.label: Struggle
narrative_stages.headline: Nearly ran out of cash before Steve Jobs's return
narrative_stages.detail: By the mid-1990s Apple was months from bankruptcy, its product lineup a confusing sprawl of overlapping computers. Steve Jobs's return in 1997 forced the company down to a handful of products it could make truly great.

narrative_stages.label: Inflection
narrative_stages.headline: The iPhone, then a second engine: high-margin Services
narrative_stages.detail: The iPhone, launched in 2007, turned Apple into the most profitable consumer electronics company in history. Over the following decade it layered a second growth engine on top — the App Store, subscriptions, and iCloud — with margins far higher than hardware and no dependence on someone buying a new phone every year.

narrative_stages.label: Today
narrative_stages.headline: Services carrying growth as iPhone matures, still the consumer-electronics leader
narrative_stages.detail: Revenue over the past year is $466.82 billion, and growth just accelerated to 16.4% in the latest quarter — unusually fast for a company this size. Net income reached $128.93 billion, up 30%, on close to a 50% gross margin. At $4.91 trillion, Apple remains the most valuable consumer electronics company by a wide margin over Microsoft, even though Nvidia's AI run recently made it the single most valuable public company overall instead of Apple.

reddit_pulse.summary_note: Illustrative example of common viewpoints in investor discussions about Apple — curated for this demo rather than a live scrape, and opinion, not fact.

thought_bubbles.take: Some investors point out that iPhone unit sales are essentially flat, and argue the recent revenue acceleration owes more to pricing, product mix, and Services than to genuine growth in new users — a distinction they think gets glossed over.

The more optimistic view is that Services has become such a large, high-margin profit engine on its own that Apple's earnings can keep compounding even in years when hardware doesn't have a breakout product.

China consistently comes up as a swing factor — both as a huge market where local phone makers are gaining ground, and as a manufacturing base that ties Apple to geopolitical and trade-policy risk it doesn't fully control.

Developers and industry watchers frequently flag antitrust pressure — from the EU's Digital Markets Act to ongoing App Store fee disputes — as a genuine long-term risk to the very Services margins that have been carrying Apple's growth story.
